PROJECT NO. 58481
CHOLLA, INC. RESPONSES TO STAFF DISCUSSION DRAFT 16 TAC §25.194
I.   INTRODUCTION
Cholla, Inc. (“Cholla”) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Staff Discussion Draft of proposed new 16 TAC §25.194 (Large Load Interconnection Standards). We thank Commission Staff for their extensive work in developing an initial framework to implement Senate Bill 6, which amends PURA through new §37.0561.
Cholla would also like to commend Commission Staff for assembling a well-structured and thoughtfully organized draft rule. The clarity of the framework greatly facilitates the ability of market participants to provide meaningful, targeted comments. This approach supports the development of a cohesive and well-considered final rule that aligns with SB6 and reflects the collective expertise of the ERCOT stakeholder community.
The growth of large loads—particularly data centers, industrial electrification, and AI compute—is reshaping the Texas grid at a pace without historical precedent. Cholla is deeply engaged in this transition as a developer of powered-land campuses across Texas. Our goal is to support reliable system growth while ensuring that Texas remains the most economically attractive jurisdiction in the country for energy-intensive investment.
We would note that SB6 strikes a careful balance among three essential objectives—supporting business development, minimizing stranded infrastructure costs, and maintaining system reliability. These three requirements operate like the three legs of a stool: each must be strong, and each must carry equal weight for the structure to stand. In implementing SB6, the Commission must balance all three legs equally to ensure a stable and durable interconnection framework.
Cholla recognizes that these comments are detailed and extensive. That length is intentional and reflects the seriousness with which we are approaching this rulemaking. The Commission is establishing regulations that will govern the development and interconnection of large loads across the ERCOT system for many years to come. These rules will directly shape how and where major investments are made, including the next generation of AI-driven data centers and advanced computing infrastructure that will help define future economic growth. It is critical to get this framework right to ensure that Texas remains a centerpiece of this development, while preserving reliability and economic efficiency at scale.
In these comments, we first highlight areas where Staff has successfully supported those three legs of the stool, and we also offer constructive alternatives in areas where additional refinement would help the rule more fully align with statutory direction, cost-causation principles, and the emerging cluster-study paradigm.

II. GENERAL COMMENTS
Cholla supports the core architecture of the Draft Rule as it reflects a good-faith effort by Commission Staff to implement PURA § 37.0561 in a manner consistent with the Legislature’s express directive to balance business development, stranded-cost risk, and system reliability. At the same time, certain structural features of the Draft Rule—particularly the sequencing of disclosures, financial commitments, and cancellation triggers—would benefit from refinement to ensure that obligations are proportionate, statutorily grounded, and aligned with the timing of ERCOT’s planning determinations.
In particular, Cholla supports: 
Defining large loads by a total peak demand equal to or greater than 75 MW.
Robust site-control requirements appropriately modeled on ERCOT’s generation interconnection framework.
Flat study fees with CPI adjustment, directly implementing PURA §37.0561(f).
Use of financial security, CIAC, long-lead equipment commitments, and other acceptable forms of financial commitment as contemplated in §37.0561(h).
Disclosure of substantially similar interconnection requests and backup-generation capability, both of which are statutory requirements rather than discretionary policy choices.
Staff’s emphasis on transparency, enforceable timelines, discipline, and improved communication throughout the LLIS and ERCOT-review process.
Establishment of an Intermediate Agreement framework to prevent indefinite occupation of planning capacity while projects remain commercially immature.
A. 	Provisional Nature of Early-Stage Large Load Information
It is important to acknowledge a fundamental characteristic of modern large load development: much of the information provided in the early stages of a project is, by necessity, provisional. For projects that will not be constructed for three years or more, a significant portion of the electrical equipment, digital infrastructure, and compute-related technologies that will ultimately be installed on the site may not yet been fully specified and in some cases, may not yet be commercialized or available. This is a vibrant and rapidly evolving industry in which material improvements occur continually, and design choices adapt in real time to technological advancements.
Because of this inherent dynamism, early-stage submissions should not be treated as fixed or final representations of a project’s final configuration. This is one of the principal reasons why a Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) system at ERCOT is so important. An LIOO platform would allow load characteristics, equipment specifications, operational parameters, and related attributes to be updated seamlessly as a project matures, rather than locking inaccurate or outdated assumptions into the interconnection process. Such a system reflects the reality of this industry far better than static, point-in-time disclosures that may be obsolete long before construction begins.
B. Necessity of a Cluster-Study Planning Framework
Further, it is important to acknowledge that a transition to a cluster-study planning framework is not merely desirable, but operationally necessary given the scale and pace of large load development now occurring in ERCOT. Cluster studies represent the only practical path forward for developing transmission solutions that are secure, efficient, and scalable for serving multiple large loads simultaneously. The current linear, project-by-project planning approach has resulted in what can only be described as a “whack-a-mole” dynamic, where individual loads are forced through multiple rounds of restudies as new projects enter the queue or advance while earlier studies are still underway. This process increases cost, delays development, and creates uncertainty without producing commensurate reliability or planning benefits.
By contrast, a cluster-study approach allows ERCOT to evaluate groups of loads together and to develop transmission solutions that are optimized across many projects at once. This enables more robust, forward-looking infrastructure planning and reduces the need for serial restudies driven by incremental changes to system conditions. From a reliability and efficiency standpoint, cluster studies are the only viable mechanism for managing the scale and pace of large load growth now occurring in ERCOT.
It appears that ERCOT intends to assume a central role in conducting these cluster studies, and Cholla supports that direction. Centralized cluster planning by ERCOT has the potential to improve coordination, consistency, and transparency, while ensuring that transmission solutions are designed to serve multiple loads in a durable and cost-effective manner.
At the same time, this transition creates an important policy consideration for this rulemaking. The rules being adopted today will either need to function effectively in a future cluster-study environment or be revisited through another rulemaking process once that transition occurs. For instance, ERCOT may perform the cluster studies themselves, which means any reference to TSPs submitting studies to ERCOT would need to be modified since they will no longer be performing them. It would be preferable—and more efficient—to craft rules now that are compatible with both the current interconnection framework and the cluster-study paradigm that ERCOT is expected to adopt.
For that reason, it would be helpful for stakeholders to receive, at a minimum, a high-level visibility into description of how ERCOT envisions the cluster-study process operating in practice. Providing this visibility would allow market participants to evaluate whether proposed requirements related to study fees, security, disclosures, milestones, and ongoing data maintenance will translate effectively into a cluster-based planning world. Without that context, there is a risk that well-intentioned rules today may not align cleanly with the planning framework of tomorrow.
C. 	Areas Requiring Adjustment	We observe several areas where adjustments are needed for the rule to align with SB6, reflect cost causation, maintain fairness, and ensure durable implementation—particularly as ERCOT’s planning framework continues to evolve toward more coordinated study approaches. Many of these issues arise from the Draft Rule’s reliance on repeated, multi-stage disclosure and securitization requirements; automatic cancellation and reallocation triggers that are untethered from actual system impacts; and open-ended ERCOT discretion that is not bounded by defined timelines or standards. Additional improvements to the rule are discussed more in-depth in our section-by-section analysis, including:
Tailoring criteria in intermediate agreements to emphasize enforceable financial and electrical commitments, with non-electrical development milestones tracked though an LIOO system at ERCOT, modeled after ERCOT’s RIOO platform used for generation resources;
Ensuring consistency in site control requirements to avoid introducing regulatory uncertainty and unnecessary financial risks at later stages of the interconnection process;
Implementing a dynamic per-MW security structure that accounts for phased development in future years, discourages artificial frontloading, and reflects the reality that near-term load causes greater system stress;
Clarifying the interpretation of "substantially similar requests" so as not to conflate similarity in size, location, or developer with speculation or duplication, where such similarities may reflect legitimate technical or architectural requirements;
Rejecting CIAC for shared network upgrades;
Accelerating the financial security refund timeline to better align with full energization; and
Allowing load participation in TSP-ERCOT study coordination calls/meetings where such participation would improve study accuracy and efficiency.
Cholla further recommends that the Commission explicitly incorporate SB6’s statutory triad—support business development, minimize stranded infrastructure costs, and maintain system reliability—either directly into subsection(a) or, at a minimum, into the Preamble accompanying the final rule, so that these statutory objectives serve as the governing interpretive principles for all future Commission ERCOT, and Transmission Service Provider decisions under this section.

III. RESPONSES TO STAFF’S QUESTIONS

Question 1. Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the commission define those parameters?

The Legislature expressly directed the Commission to require disclosure of substantially similar interconnection requests whose approval could materially alter the request at hand. Cholla supports this requirement as a transparency safeguard, not as a substitute for speculation screening. This disclosure obligation should be implemented consistent with PURA § 37.0561(d) as a targeted, informational requirement, and not expanded into repeated certifications or heightened detail beyond what the statute authorizes.
At the same time, determining whether requests are “substantially similar” requires careful, fact-specific judgment. Developers frequently pursue multiple proximate sites of similar size as part of deliberate, technically driven deployment strategies involving latency, redundancy, modularity, and scalability. Similarity of size, geography, or the identity of a large load alone does not indicate duplication or queue gaming, nor does the absence of a prematurely executed retail service agreement with the certificated provider of retail service.
Cholla has observed instances in other markets where large customers submitted numerous interconnection requests and later withdrew many of them upon securing only a preferred subset creating substantial inefficiencies  and unnecessary workload for transmission planners. Requiring disclosure of substatantially similar requests may help deter this type of behavior, though meaningful financial securitization is likely the more effective tool for discouraging duplicate requests.
It is also important to recognize that many apparently similar requests reflect intentional and technically necessary development strategies, not speculation. Hyperscale and large-compute architectures often require multiple nearby sites to support low-latency operations, workload distribution, redundancy, and long-term scalability. In these contexts, what may appear duplicative in isolation is frequently a coordinated component of a single development strategy.For these reasons, Cholla encourages the Commission to 
avoid rigid or mechanical definitions and instead apply this requirement narrowly and functionally, focusing on whether approval of another request would actually result in a material change, delay, or withdrawal of the request at issue. Similarity in location, megawatt size, or developer identity, standing alone, should not be treated as determinative.

Question 2. Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific information related to a substantially similar interconnection request and allow anonymization of competitively sensitive details. Should the commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive? If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?
Cholla supports the requirement in proposed §§25.194(c)(3) and (e)(3) for disclosure of substantially similar interconnection requests, as this requirement is expressly contemplated by SB6 and serves an important planning and transparency function. Cholla also supports allowing anonymization of competitively sensitive information, as premature or unnecessary disclosure of such information could undermine legitimate development activity without improving ERCOT’s ability to identify duplicative or non-viable requests.
With respect to whether the Commission should enumerate what is and is not competitively sensitive, a principles-based approach is preferable to an exhaustive or rigid list. Large-load development strategies vary widely, and an overly prescriptive definition risks becoming outdated or inadvertently exposing sensitive information as technologies and business models evolve.
That said, it would be helpful for the Commission to provide high-level guidance distinguishing between:
(1) information that ERCOT and the Transmission Service Provider need in order to assess potential duplication or queue interaction, and
(2) information that should remain anonymized or aggregated due to its commercial sensitivity or CEII classification.
The following categories of information are generally necessary for ERCOT and the TSP to assess whether interconnection requests are substantially similar, but should be provided only in anonymized and aggregated form, consistent with ERCOT’s treatment of load data as highly sensitive:
Approximate geographic area expressed at a high level (e.g., transmission zone, county, or general substation area, without parcel-level detail);
Requested MW magnitude or MW range, expressed in rounded or banded values;
General timing category for energization (e.g., near-term, mid-term, later-year), rather than specific dates;
Whether requests are associated with the same applicant or affiliated entities, without disclosure of confidential commercial relationships; and
Whether projects are intended to be mutually exclusive or capable of proceeding concurrently.
This level of disclosure allows ERCOT and the TSP to understand planning interactions and potential duplication while preserving confidentiality and avoiding unnecessary exposure of sensitive load information.
Information Generally Considered Competitively Sensitive and Appropriate for Anonymization
The following categories of information are typically competitively sensitive and/or CEII, and should remain anonymized or withheld from broader disclosure:
Exact site locations, parcel identifiers, or property boundaries;
Specific customer identities, tenant names, or hyperscaler relationships;
Detailed commercial terms, pricing, or internal development prioritization;
Proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies (including latency-driven clustering concepts); and
Confidential financing structures, capital allocation decisions, or internal approval thresholds.
Disclosure of this information is not necessary for ERCOT or the TSP to determine whether requests are substantially similar, nor does it materially improve the ability to assess whether a request is unlikely to materialize.
Cholla reiterates that, as mentioned above similarity in MW size, general location, or applicant affiliation does not, by itself, indicate speculation or duplication. Accordingly, any guidance on competitively sensitive information should be paired with clear recognition that the disclosure requirement is intended to support planning and transparency, not to penalize legitimate multi-site development strategies or require premature public disclosure of confidential load information.
Finally, as ERCOT transitions toward a Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) tracking system, much of the information relevant to substantially similar requests can be maintained internally within ERCOT on a confidential basis. Under such a framework, ERCOT would have continuous, CEII-protected visibility into project status, affiliations, and changes over time, reducing reliance on repeated manual disclosures and further mitigating concerns regarding disclosure of sensitive load information.

Question 3. Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting utility and ERCOT of any change to information initially disclosed, or only material changes? If only material changes, how should “material change” be defined?
The Commission should require notification only of material changes to information initially disclosed. It is appropriate for the Commission to identify illustrative examples of what may constitute a “material change,” while avoiding an exhaustive or rigid definition. Whether a change is material should be evaluated based on whether it meaningfully affects ERCOT’s planning assumptions, study results, or the need for transmission facilities. Examples of changes that would generally be considered material include, but are not limited to:
Changes in requested capacity, including increases or reductions in total MW that would alter study results, facilities scope, or transmission upgrade requirements;
Material changes to the load ramp or energization timeline, particularly where near-term load is delayed or accelerated in a way that affects the sequencing or necessity of transmission projects;
Changes in the nature or operational characteristics of the load, such as a shift between materially different load types (for example, from a data center to a Bitcoin mining facility, or vice versa) where the change affects load shape, controllability, duty cycle, or dynamic behavior;
Changes in ownership or control of the project or site, including transfers that alter the party responsible for financial security, operational decisions, or contractual commitments;
Loss, expiration, or material modification of site control, such that the project’s physical location or feasibility is no longer consistent with the assumptions used in the studies;
Material changes to backup generation configuration or operating characteristics, where those changes affect net load at the Point of Interconnection or alter contingency or emergency-operation assumptions relied upon in planning studies.
Requiring notice of every minor or technical update would be administratively burdensome, would not meaningfully improve planning outcomes, and would be inconsistent with the inherently iterative nature of large load development. Nothing in PURA § 37.0561 requires continuous re-disclosure of immaterial changes, and imposing such an obligation would convert an informational statute into an ongoing compliance regime untethered from planning relevance.
In determining materiality, the Commission should focus on whether a change could reasonably affect transmission planning assumptions, study outcomes, cost allocation, or interconnection timing. Changes that merely refine design details or reflect routine project maturation should not, standing alone, trigger mandatory notice obligations.
In this context, Cholla encourages the Commission to consider the broader evolution of ERCOT’s load-interconnection processes toward more dynamic information management. ERCOT is expected to move toward a Load Integration and Ongoing Operation (LIOO) tracking system—analogous to the Resource Integration and Ongoing Operations (RIOO) platform used for generation resources. Under such a system, ERCOT could maintain a unified, continuously updated project record for each large load, including:
Project developer identity,
End-use customer identity (if different),
Commercial arrangements affecting load delivery,
Site characteristics relevant to interconnection,
Backup-generation attributes,
Ramp schedules, and
Changes in ownership or control over the course of development.

Within such a framework, the project-developer/end-user designation would remain constant throughout the interconnection lifecycle unless a commercial transfer occurs. Only changes that alter the identity of the responsible counterparty, the magnitude or timing of load, the existence or characteristics of backup generation, or other inputs used in transmission studies should be deemed material. When such changes occur, the LIOO record would require an update—just as RIOO does for generation—ensuring that ERCOT and the TSP have accurate and current information without imposing unnecessary re-filing obligations.

Question 4. Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting utility to refund 20% of a customer’s security after energization and ratably as the customer meets phased-energization milestones. Should the commission standardize the rate for milestone-based refunds? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund? 
Cholla supports the concept that financial security should be refunded over time as load is energized and transmission facilities are placed into productive use. This approach appropriately reflects the gradual ramping typical of large load projects and aligns the release of security with actual system utilization. 
However, the refund framework as drafted is misaligned with real-world development timelines and would benefit from refinement. A structure that delays full repayment for five (5) years after full energization imposes a substantial financial burden that is disconnected from actual system risk. By the time a project has reached full energization, the transmission facilities serving it are in operation, the risk of non-performance has largely been eliminated, and the original purpose of the security—protecting against stranded investment—has been satisfied. Extending security retention beyond full energization effectively transforms a protective mechanism into a financing tool, a result not contemplated by PURA and inconsistent with cost-causation principles.
Cholla therefore recommends that the Commission standardize full repayment of financial security occurs at or near full energization, rather than tying repayment to an additional multi-year holding period. Interim refunds should remain tied to objective, measurable electrical milestones, such as incremental megawatt energization and achievement of full registered capacity.
While a relatively simple approach may be preferred, any standardized refund structure should also be administratively workable and flexible enough to accommodate diverse ramp profiles. Overly complex formulas increase administrative burden without improving outcomes. A milestone-based framework grounded in electrical performance (e.g., incremental MW energization; completion of full registered capacity) provides clarity, predictability, and protection against stranded costs while avoiding unnecessary capital lockup. 
Accordingly, Cholla respectfully recommends that §25.194(k) be revised to provide for full repayment of financial security at or near full energization, with interim refunds tied to ramp milestones, rather than conditioning repayment on an additional post-energization holding period.

Question 5. Are changes to other substantive Commission rules necessary to align with this rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made and to which rules?
Please see Cholla’s section-by-section comments below for recommended changes.

IV. RECOMMENDED CHANGES TO PROPOSED 16 TAC § 25.194
§25.194(a) Purpose and Scope
We respectfully recommend that the Commission explicitly incorporate SB6’s statutory triad—support business development, minimize stranded infrastructure costs, and maintain system reliability—either directly into subsection (a) or, at a minimum, into the Preamble accompanying the final rule, so that it serves as the guiding interpretive principle for all future Commission, ERCOT, and TSP decisions under this section. Including this statutory purpose statement in the rule or Preamble will help ensure that implementation of §25.194 remains aligned with the Legislature’s intent and provides a balanced framework for long-term interconnection policy and transmission planning.
§25.194(c) Disclosures and Study Fee
Cholla supports the disclosure requirement to differentiate between a project developer and an end-use customer, as it provides helpful clarity to the TSP and ERCOT regarding the nature of the party initiating the interconnection request. Better visibility into project structure can improve communication and reduce misunderstandings throughout the interconnection process. However, it is important that this distinction not introduce—either explicitly or implicitly—any bias in favor of end-users over project developers. The data-center industry relies on a wide range of valid development models, all of which contribute meaningfully to ERCOT’s rapid load growth:
Some hyperscalers conduct site identification, acquisition, and full development entirely in-house.
Some co-location providers independently identify sites, develop and construct facilities, and then lease capacity to hyperscalers.
Some companies—such as Cholla—specialize in identifying strategic locations, acquiring property, performing technical and environmental due diligence (including interconnection requests), and then selling fully diligenced powered-land sites to hyperscalers or co-locators.
Some projects originate with landowners who have transmission lines or substations on or near their property.
These parties also have varying levels of sophistication and play distinct but equally important roles in the value chain that takes a data center from concept to construction. Developers may have deep expertise in land acquisition, due diligence, permitting, and early-stage interconnection work, while hyperscalers and co-locators bring their own internal engineering, architectural, and operational expertise.
All of these business models are valid and essential components of the development ecosystem. None should be implicitly favored or disadvantaged. The purpose of this disclosure should be strictly informational—to clarify who is initiating the request—not to create a hierarchy or suggest greater legitimacy of one participant over another. Cholla therefore urges the Commission to ensure that this disclosure remains neutral and is not interpreted in a way that would afford any class of participant an advantage in the interconnection process.

§25.194(c)(2) Site Control
Cholla supports this requirement and for consistency recommends aligning acceptable site-control documentation with ERCOT Planning Guide §5.3.2, which allows:
Fee simple ownership,
Executed lease agreements with appropriate control rights,
Exclusive options supported by consideration, or
Executed purchase-and-sale agreements (PSAs).

§25.194(c)(3) Substantially Similar Requests
Cholla supports this subsection because it aligns directly with the statutory requirement in SB6 §37.0561(d). The Legislature expressly directed the Commission to require disclosure of whether the customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request elsewhere in Texas whose approval might materially change, delay, or withdraw the request at hand.
However, we would also emphasize that determining whether requests are “substantially similar” can be complex. Developers often intentionally pursue multiple sites with similar size and characteristics in the same general area. This is not speculative behavior—it reflects deliberate, purpose-driven architectural decisions.
For these reasons, while Cholla supports the inclusion of this subsection, we encourage the Commission and TSPs to interpret this requirement carefully, recognizing that similarity of location, MW quantity, or developer identity, by themselves, do not equate to duplication or speculation. The rule should be applied with nuance so as not to penalize or mischaracterize legitimate hyperscale development approaches.
§25.194(c)(4) Schedule for Phased Energization
Cholla supports requiring a phased energization schedule as part of a large-load interconnection request and agrees that this information is an important planning input. Cholla further supports the use of this schedule by ERCOT and the Transmission Service Provider in both steady-state and dynamic studies, as doing so improves study accuracy and better reflects the expected operational profile of large loads over time.
At the same time, it is critical to recognize that early-stage energization schedules are inherently provisional. Large-load ramping depends on numerous factors, including construction sequencing, equipment availability, technology selection, customer demand, financing conditions, and permitting timelines. Many of these factors evolve materially after the initial interconnection request is submitted and are often outside the control of the interconnecting customer.
In practice, the actual availability of electrical capacity is frequently driven by the completion of transmission facilities, rather than by a developer’s preferred production or installation timeline. As a result, load ramping often occurs in discrete blocks or steps, corresponding to when transmission upgrades, substations, or line reinforcements are placed into service, rather than as a smooth or continuous increase.
Developers also approach this reality differently. Some developers choose to install equipment in advance and remain idle or lightly loaded until additional capacity is released, while others construct only the underlying infrastructure and defer installation of computing equipment until transmission capacity is formally made available. Both approaches are rational responses to the same underlying constraint: electrical capacity is released by the grid in increments, not continuously.
For these reasons, phased energization schedules should be treated as planning assumptions rather than binding commitments, particularly in the early stages of the interconnection process. The rule should not create incentives for applicants to over-specify near-term ramping but rather support creation of load profiles that best reflect how capacity is actually delivered.
The interconnection framework should explicitly anticipate and accommodate stepwise updates to energization schedules as transmission facilities are completed and capacity is released. In this regard, a dynamic data-management approach—such as the Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) system contemplated by ERCOT—would allow ramp schedules to be updated in a structured and transparent manner as projects progress, better aligning planning assumptions with real-world conditions.

§25.194(c)(5) Backup Generation
Cholla supports Staff’s inclusion of this disclosure requirement, which aligns directly with SB6 §37.0561(e). Knowing whether backup generation exists—and its size and operating characteristics—helps ERCOT and the TSP understand how the load may behave during system stress events. Additionally, incorporating backup generation capability into ERCOT’s planning models, steady-state and dynamic cases, and long-term resource adequacy forecasting would offer meaningful visibility into how these assets contribute to system resilience. While such integration may fall outside the scope of this rulemaking, it is a valuable consideration for future ERCOT or Commission initiatives.

§25.194(c)(6) Dynamic Modeling
Cholla supports the requirement for dynamic modeling information as an essential component of ERCOT’s and the Transmission Service Providers’ ability to evaluate system stability, fault response, short-circuit duties, and ride-through performance for large loads. As large loads become a more material component of ERCOT demand, understanding their dynamic behavior during system disturbances is critical to maintaining reliability.
At the same time, it is important to recognize that dynamic load models for large loads—particularly data centers—are inherently iterative and evolve over time. Dynamic behavior is closely tied to equipment selection, control strategies, protection schemes, and interactions with backup generation and uninterruptible power supplies. For projects with multi-year development horizons, many of these elements may not yet be finalized at the time of the initial interconnection request, and in some cases the specific technologies to be deployed may not yet exist.
For this reason, early-stage dynamic models should be understood as best-available representations based on current design assumptions, rather than as final or immutable specifications. ERCOT and the Transmission Service Providers should expect that dynamic modeling data will be updated as projects mature, equipment selections are finalized, and operating strategies are refined.
The rule should explicitly accommodate this iterative process and avoid treating early dynamic models as compliance certifications. Doing so will encourage more accurate and transparent modeling over time and reduce incentives for applicants to over-constrain or misrepresent expected behavior simply to satisfy early-stage requirements.
In this regard, a dynamic data-management framework—such as the Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) system contemplated by ERCOT—would allow dynamic modeling information to be maintained and updated in a structured manner as projects progress, improving model fidelity while aligning expectations with real-world development timelines.

§25.194(c)(7) Study Fee
Cholla supports Staff’s implementation of the flat study-fee requirement mandated under SB6 §37.0561(f). Establishing a clear, uniform minimum study fee provides transparency, supports predictability, and serves an important gatekeeping function by ensuring that interconnection requests reflect a baseline level of seriousness and commitment.
Cholla also agrees that a flat study fee helps align developer expectations with the resources required by ERCOT and the Transmission Service Providers to perform Large Load Interconnection Studies. Clear upfront cost signals reduce uncertainty and improve planning efficiency for all parties.
However, Cholla notes that a significant portion of the study costs being incurred today is driven not by the intrinsic complexity of individual projects, but by repeated restudies under ERCOT’s existing linear planning structure. These restudies are frequently triggered by model updates, queue reordering, and the advancement of other projects, rather than by changes to the underlying interconnection request. The result is increased workload, extended timelines, and higher cumulative study costs.
Looking ahead, as ERCOT transitions toward a centralized cluster-study methodology, the nature of study work and its cost drivers will change. Under a cluster framework, ERCOT will likely assume a greater role in coordinating grouped studies, which may require additional engineering resources, enhanced modeling environments, and new software tools to support that function effectively.
Once cluster studies become the dominant planning approach, the flat study-fee structure may need to be reevaluated to ensure it continues to:
Reflect actual ERCOT and TSP study costs,
Support the staffing and tools necessary to manage cluster planning,
Reduce the churn associated with serial restudies, and
Maintain predictable interconnection timelines.
It is therefore appropriate for the Commission to revisit the study-fee framework as part of the broader transition to cluster-based planning, to ensure the fee remains aligned with actual planning costs and continues to serve its intended purpose.
Therefore, the rule should be written with sufficient flexibility to allow for potential recalibration of the study-fee structure following the implementation of cluster studies. While such recalibration may ultimately prove unnecessary if planning costs do not change materially, the transition to a clustered planning framework represents a fundamental overhaul of today’s interconnection process, and it is reasonable to anticipate that underlying cost drivers could evolve. Preserving the ability to revisit and adjust the study-fee structure, if warranted, will help ensure the rule remains durable, responsive, and aligned with actual planning costs over time.

§25.194(d) Large Load Interconnection Study
Cholla strongly supports Staff’s introduction of explicit timeline requirements and transparency into the LLIS process. These improvements help ensure that studies move forward predictably, reduce uncertainty for developers, and provide clearer signals for capital commitments.
In addition, Cholla recommends allowing the requesting load to participate in LLIS coordination calls between the TSP and ERCOT. Cholla has experienced this firsthand with one TSP that voluntarily included us in their study calls. Being part of the conversation materially improved study clarity and allowed us to explain the scope and phasing of the project directly, respond to questions in real time, clarify modeling assumptions, and help prevent misunderstandings that can lead to unnecessary restudies.
Allowing load participation—at the discretion of the TSP and ERCOT—would not change study responsibilities but would significantly enhance communication, reduce delays, and improve study accuracy. This recommendation complements the transparency measures already proposed and aligns with SB6’s goals of supporting business development and maintaining reliability.
As with other sections of this rule, it would be wise for the Commission to preserve sufficient flexibility in the language to allow the functionality of this structure to be revisited once ERCOT has adopted a cluster-study planning process. The transition to clustered studies may alter study sequencing, coordination practices, and information flows, and ensuring the rule can adapt to that future framework will help avoid unnecessary rigidity or the need for additional rulemakings.

§25.194(e) Discretionary Services Agreement
Cholla recommends striking §25.194(e)(1) in its entirety because the information required here is duplicative of the disclosure already provided under §25.194(c)(1), and repeating it offers no additional value at the DSA stage, creates potential for confusion if the two disclosures appear inconsistent, and does not enhance the accuracy or quality of the LLIS. The identity of the party initiating the interconnection request — whether a project developer, an end-use customer, a co-location operator, or a landowner — is fully and accurately captured earlier in the process. No material change typically occurs between the initial submission and DSA execution.
The Commission should also consider the broader evolution of ERCOT’s load-interconnection processes. ERCOT is expected to move toward a Load Integration and Ongoing Operation (LIOO) tracking system—analogous to the Resource Integration and Ongoing Operations (RIOO) platform used for generation resources. Under such a system, ERCOT could maintain a unified, continuously updated record for each large load, including:
Project developer identity,
End-use customer identity (if different),
Commercial arrangements,
Modeling data,
Site characteristics,
Backup-generation attributes,
Ramp schedules,
And any changes in ownership or control throughout development.
In such a framework, the project-developer/end-user designation would remain constant throughout the interconnection lifecycle unless a commercial transfer occurs. When a transfer does occur, the LIOO system would require an update—just as RIOO does for generation—ensuring that ERCOT and the TSP have accurate, up-to-date insight into project sponsorship.
(e)(2) Site Control
Cholla reiterates that a site option almost always includes a due diligence period, and the primary purpose of that due diligence is to determine whether electrical power can realistically be delivered to the location. This is the central gating factor in the development of large-load campuses. Because ERCOT’s LLIS/Planning Review process can ultimately determine that power is not deliverable to the site, it does not make practical or commercial sense to require a customer to convert an option into full ownership or a long-term lease before ERCOT has confirmed that transmission service is even feasible. Requiring ownership prior to a deliverability determination forces customers to assume irreversible land-acquisition obligations for sites that ERCOT may later find electrically infeasible — an outcome that would undermine SB6’s directive to support business development and avoid unnecessary early financial exposure.
For these reasons, Cholla recommends that the Commission allow options, leases, or executed purchase agreements to satisfy site-control requirements at this stage, provided the instrument remains valid through a meaningful, ERCOT-reviewed energization milestone. This approach ensures that projects are serious and commercially grounded, while avoiding requirements that force premature land acquisition before ERCOT determines feasibility.

(e)(3) Substantially Similar Requests
Cholla understands the need for this requirement because it is entirely possible for additional properties to be acquired or evaluated between the time of the initial filing and the point at which ERCOT and the TSP begin the study process. For this reason, we support reaffirming this disclosure at the DSA stage, as it ensures ERCOT and the TSP have current and accurate information about the customer’s siting activities before studies are initiated.
It is also important to recognize the direction ERCOT is heading. Once ERCOT adopts a Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) system analogous to the RIOO platform used for generation resources, this type of disclosure should be automatically captured within the system. Under an LIOO framework, the filing load will have a standing responsibility to update the project record whenever a material change occurs — including the acquisition of additional potential sites or the withdrawal of previously contemplated ones. In such a system, the status of “substantially similar requests” becomes an ongoing data attribute managed within ERCOT’s tracking platform, rather than a repeated manual disclosure at multiple stages of the process.
With respect to interpretation, Cholla refers the Commission back to our earlier discussion under §25.194(c)(3), where we explained in detail that many apparent similarities between sites reflect intentional, purpose-driven architectural and operational decisions rather than duplicative or speculative queue behavior. Those points remain fully valid here and apply equally at the DSA stage. This subsection should be interpreted in a manner that recognizes the legitimate technical and commercial reasons for multi-site development while still fulfilling SB6’s transparency mandate.

(e)(4) Site-Related Studies
Cholla does not support the inclusion of this requirement because it is not required by SB6, and its placement here does not appear to meaningfully advance the objectives of the statute or prove viability. A large load may submit a request expecting power to be available in two years, only to learn — after ERCOT’s studies are complete — that power cannot be delivered for five years or more.
Because electrical feasibility and timeline drive every other development decision, none of the elements referenced here (air permitting, water or wastewater studies, civil or traffic analysis, or related site-planning studies) are typically initiated until the developer knows when and whether power will be available. Developers do not begin these processes in earnest until the LLIS and ERCOT Planning Review establish a viable path and timeline for interconnection.
This means that in the early stage of development that ERCOT and the TSP are requesting such materials, much of the information will be incomplete and of limited value. Initiating such studies prematurely would be financially imprudent and misaligned with real-world development sequencing.
Additionally, these subject areas fall outside the expertise of TSP and ERCOT staff. They do not work in water engineering, wastewater system design, air permitting, geotechnical review, or civil infrastructure planning. Evaluating these studies would require external specialists, and it is unclear what ERCOT or a TSP could meaningfully infer from such materials at this stage.
For these reasons, and because SB6 does not require such disclosures, Cholla does not support the inclusion of §25.194(e)(4). This requirement at this stage of early development imposes an administrative burden without providing actionable insight and risks introducing uncertainty into an already backlogged interconnection process.

(e)(5) State and Local Regulatory Approvals
Cholla similarly does not support this requirement because SB6 does not require it, and its practical usefulness is limited. Electrical power availability remains the first and most consequential gating factor in determining whether a site can progress toward development. Developers do not meaningfully begin the processes of air permitting, municipal construction permitting, zoning actions, subdivision approvals, or environmental compliance until they understand when the site can be energized.
Given this sequencing, at the point ERCOT and the TSP request these materials, few, if any, regulatory approvals will have been initiated, and the absence of such approvals does not indicate that a project is not advancing. The information available, or lack thereof, provides little insight into interconnection feasibility or project readiness.
Further, as with §25.194(e)(4), ERCOT and TSP personnel do not have the background required to interpret these materials, nor do they have statutory authority to evaluate municipal, county, or state-level permitting adequacy. These processes involve distinct regulatory bodies, professional disciplines, and local jurisdictions.
Consequently, because SB6 does not require this disclosure, and because the information would typically not exist at this stage and would not materially inform ERCOT or TSP study processes, Cholla does not support the inclusion of §25.194(e)(5) in the final rule.

(e)(6) Load Schedule
Cholla supports requiring an updated load schedule at this stage. This ensures that ERCOT and the TSPs incorporate the most accurate and current ramp profile into LLIS modeling and infrastructure-scope determinations. Load schedules often evolve as commercial commitments solidify and as developers refine campus phasing, power requirements, and internal commissioning plans. Ensuring that ERCOT and the TSPs are using the most current information at the DSA stage improves the accuracy of both steady-state and dynamic studies.
Furthermore, as with other disclosures, once ERCOT adopts a Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) system analogous to the RIOO platform for generation, this load schedule should be maintained and updated on a continual basis by the applicant. In such a framework, the load schedule becomes part of an ongoing project record rather than a single point-in-time submission at increasingly later stages of the interconnection process. This avoids duplicative re-filing of unchanged information and ensures ERCOT always has the most current version available.
(e)(7) Backup Generation
Cholla supports requiring updated backup-generation information at this stage. Backup-generation plans often evolve as site due diligence progresses, as internal resiliency standards are finalized, or as equipment procurement decisions change. Providing the TSP and ERCOT with updated backup-generation details enhances the accuracy of LLIS, informs fault analysis and emergency-operation scenarios, and strengthens planning assumptions for contingency events.
Backup-generation information is also particularly valuable because it provides ERCOT with situational awareness regarding loads that have on-site generation available and the extent to which that resource may reduce net load at the Point of Interconnection under certain operating conditions. Understanding the presence, capacity, and operating characteristics of backup generation allows ERCOT to better assess how large loads may behave during system stress events and how net demand at specific locations could change dynamically.
As with the load schedule, once ERCOT adopts a Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) tracking system, backup-generation information should be updated on a continual basis by the applicant. Under such a system, backup-generation attributes would be maintained as part of ERCOT’s ongoing project record and would be updated whenever equipment specifications, operating configurations, or generation capacities change. This approach eliminates duplicative disclosures, ensures ERCOT’s models reflect current conditions at all times, and aligns backup-generation tracking with the workflow ERCOT already uses for generation resources under RIOO.

(e)(8) Financial Security ($/MW)
Cholla agrees with Commission Staff that a per-MW financial commitment is an appropriate and constructive tool for demonstrating project seriousness. We view the move to a per-MW structure as a positive development because it naturally disciplines the size of the interconnection request: larger requests produce proportionately larger financial commitments, reducing the incentive to overstate load. At the same time, the design of this requirement is critically important. A poorly calibrated per-MW amount — or one that lacks a timing element — can distort customer behavior, encourage unrealistic ramp profiles, and misalign incentives between developers, ERCOT, and TSPs.
A per-MW security requirement should target the actual magnitude of interconnection-related securitization and CIAC obligations that a project will ultimately face after the LLIS and facilities-scope determination phases. Larger loads typically drive proportionately larger upgrade requirements and corresponding security postings. A security structure that meaningfully approximates those ultimate obligations serves two essential purposes:
(1) it screens out requests that cannot realistically be financed, and
(2) it ensures the entities entering the queue understand, from the start, the financial seriousness of the interconnection path they are embarking on.
Cholla recommends that Commission Staff poll the TSPs — using recent LLIS cases, facilities studies, and executed agreements — to estimate the typical range of securitization and CIAC costs expressed in $/MW terms. This empirical approach ensures that the security structure reflects real-world experience rather than a static or arbitrary number. In our earlier comments, Cholla offered an example structure beginning at approximately $10,000/MW and declining 20% per year over a multiyear energization schedule. This structure is intended to reflect the following principles:
Near-term load creates greater system stress and offers fewer opportunities for coordinated optimization with other projects.
Later-year load allows ERCOT more flexibility to incorporate the project into broader planning processes, particularly once cluster studies are adopted.
A declining per-MW structure discourages front-loading of energy ramps solely to obtain perceived queue priority.
Aligning the initial financial commitment with eventual securitization requirements helps ensure that only financially viable projects remain in the interconnection process.
Furthermore, the initial per-MW security should be fully creditable toward subsequent obligations — including CIAC, long-lead equipment security, and network-upgrade security — so that customers are not double-charged. This ensures that the initial security functions as the first installment of the project’s total financial commitment, rather than as a standalone or additive requirement.
Finally, Cholla notes that the sequencing contemplated in §25.194(g)—including the requirement that financial security be posted before study results are transmitted to ERCOT—reflects a process in which the Transmission Service Provider performs and submits individual Large Load Interconnection Studies. As ERCOT transitions toward a cluster-study planning paradigm, it is likely that ERCOT will assume a more direct role in performing and coordinating studies, which may alter the timing, sequencing, and functional role of security posting relative to study completion and submission. For this reason, the rule should be structured with sufficient flexibility to allow this framework to be revisited and revised as the cluster-study process is implemented, so that study execution and security requirements remain appropriately aligned with the entity performing the analysis and the objectives of coordinated, system-wide planning.
§25.194(f) Submission of LLIS to ERCOT
Cholla recommends that §25.194(f) be reorganized to more clearly reflect the intended sequence of events following completion of the Large Load Interconnection Study. Presenting this section as an ordered set of obligations will improve clarity, reduce ambiguity, and ensure consistent application across Transmission Service Providers.
Specifically, Cholla recommends structuring this subsection to provide that:
Once the transmission studies have been completed, the requesting load shall have 30 days to post the required Discretionary Services Agreement financial security.
If the load posts the required security within that 30-day window, the Transmission Service Provider shall have 7 days to submit the completed study results and associated materials to ERCOT.
If the load does not post the required security within the 30-day window, the Transmission Service Provider shall have 30 days to notify ERCOT that the project has been canceled.
Cholla supports the inclusion of a 30-day deadline for posting DSA security. While this is a relatively short period, its inclusion in the rule is important because it establishes a clear, enforceable milestone that brings discipline and predictability to the interconnection process. The existence of a firm deadline ensures that projects do not linger indefinitely following study completion and that ERCOT and the TSP can advance planning decisions with confidence.
The presence of this deadline also appropriately places responsibility on the load to prepare in advance for study completion. Loads should reasonably anticipate the conclusion of studies and arrange internal approvals, financing, and security instruments accordingly, rather than waiting until after studies are finalized.
That said, this structure would benefit from an explicit notification requirement. To support compliance with the 30-day posting window, Cholla recommends that the rule require the Transmission Service Provider to notify the load when the studies are within 30 days of completion. Providing such notice will help ensure that the load has adequate visibility into timing, reduce the risk of inadvertent non-compliance, and further support the orderly transition from study completion to ERCOT submission or project withdrawal.
Finally, Cholla notes that the sequencing contemplated in §25.194(g)—including the requirement that financial security be posted before study results are transmitted to ERCOT—reflects a process in which the Transmission Service Provider performs and submits individual Large Load Interconnection Studies. As ERCOT transitions toward a cluster-study planning paradigm, it is expected that the set of transmission projects identified in one cluster study will form the starting point for the subsequent cluster study. Because the time between cluster-study cycles is likely to be relatively tight, it is critical that the list of transmission projects carried forward accurately reflects the set of loads that have posted security and are genuinely moving forward.
In this context, clear and timely confirmation of which loads have posted security becomes essential to maintaining an accurate transmission framework for the next study cycle. If a material number of loads do not post their required security, many transmission projects identified in a prior study may no longer be needed and should not be carried forward. Ensuring that only supported transmission projects advance into subsequent cluster studies will improve planning accuracy, reduce unnecessary analysis, and allow ERCOT to develop durable, system-wide solutions based on a reliable set of committed loads.
For these reasons, the rule should be structured with sufficient flexibility to allow this framework to be revisited and refined as the cluster-study process is implemented, so that study execution, security requirements, and inter-study sequencing remain properly aligned with coordinated, system-wide planning objectives.

§25.194(g) Notification of Additional Study
Cholla strongly supports the intent of §25.194(g) to improve transparency and predictability regarding when additional studies are required. Clear and timely notification of the need for additional study is essential to maintaining confidence in the interconnection process and allowing projects to make informed business decisions.
This provision is particularly important given the current planning environment in ERCOT. Under the existing linear study paradigm, large-load projects are frequently subjected to multiple rounds of restudies driven by incremental changes in system conditions, model updates, or the advancement of other projects in the queue. These restudies can materially affect cost, timing, and feasibility, often with limited advance warning.
For these reasons, Cholla supports requiring ERCOT and the Transmission Service Provider to provide prompt notification when an additional study is required, along with a clear explanation of the basis for that determination. Early visibility into the drivers of a restudy allows projects to assess the implications, adjust expectations, and coordinate internally on next steps. Furthermore, the criteria for requiring additional studies should be anchored to objective planning standards wherever possible, rather than left to open-ended discretion. Tying restudy triggers to defined thresholds or conditions in ERCOT’s Planning Guides will help reduce uncertainty and limit unnecessary restudy churn.
§25.194(h) Intermediate Agreement
The Intermediate Agreement should serve a narrow and well-defined purpose: marking the transition from transmission planning to construction by requiring enforceable financial and electrical commitments. The Intermediate Agreement should not function as a general development-status checkpoint or as a repository for information that is duplicative, non-electrical, or inherently dynamic. When structured properly, §25.194(h) can provide clarity, discipline, and protection against stranded investment while remaining compatible with ERCOT’s evolving planning frameworks, including LIOO and future cluster studies.

§25.194(h)(1)–(7): Informational and Redundant Requirements
Cholla recommends that §25.194(h)(1) through §25.194(h)(7) be struck or relocated. These subsections largely consist of informational updates, confirmations, or development-stage indicators that:
Duplicate disclosures already required in the interconnection process (including under §§25.194(c) and (e));
Are inherently subject to change and therefore inappropriate to freeze at a single contractual milestone; or
Describe activities and conditions already monitored through ERCOT and TSP processes independent of this rule.
Much of the information contemplated in §§25.194(h)(1)–(7) will evolve over multi-year development timelines in an industry characterized by rapid technological change. As discussed elsewhere in these comments, such information is more appropriately maintained through ERCOT’s evolving Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO) framework, where it can be updated on a continual basis rather than restated at successive rule-defined checkpoints.
Retaining §§25.194(h)(1)–(7) in the Intermediate Agreement section adds administrative burden without improving enforceability, reliability, or planning accuracy. It also blurs the purpose of the Intermediate Agreement, which should be focused on financial commitment and electrical readiness, not non-electrical development milestones.
CIAC, Network Upgrades, and “Fair Share” Cost Allocation
Cholla understands and supports the underlying policy objective reflected in SB6: ensuring that large loads pay their fair share of transmission costs associated with serving them. However, CIAC is not the appropriate mechanism to achieve that objective, and Cholla does not find anything in SB6 requiring or supporting the use of CIAC to replace or replicate system-wide transmission cost recovery. SB6 explicitly directed the Commission to review transmission cost allocation rules, including the Four Coincident Peak (4CP) mechanism, as the appropriate vehicle for addressing concerns about whether large loads are contributing proportionately to the transmission system. That directive reflects a recognition that system transmission costs are best allocated through system-wide rate design, not through project-specific CIAC constructs. Attempting to force “fair share” cost recovery through CIAC creates a series of fundamental problems.
First, CIAC is incompatible with ongoing TCOS recovery. If a large load is required to fund the bulk of a transmission upgrade through CIAC, it is not economically or legally coherent to then also charge that same load ongoing TCOS based on 4CP or other system metrics. Doing so would result in reverse subsidization, where the load both pays for the asset upfront and continues to pay for it again through rates, while other users benefit without equivalent contribution.
Second, the Draft Rule’s attempt to address this issue through a concept of subsequent compensation by later-connecting large loads is not workable. Transmission facilities are constructed to satisfy multiple contingency cases across a wide range of system conditions. Determining “how much” of a line or upgrade is used by a second or third load across dozens or hundreds of contingencies would require arbitrary allocation assumptions, highly subjective modeling judgments, and continual recalculation as new loads interconnect. This quickly devolves into an incomprehensible accounting exercise, with no clear answer as to how compensation would be calculated, tracked, or revisited over time.
Third, and equally problematic, the Draft Rule’s compensation construct appears to apply only to subsequent large loads. Under this approach, only later-connecting large loads would be required to compensate the original load that funded the upgrade, while all other loads—including smaller commercial, industrial, and residential customers—would use the upgraded transmission facilities without providing any compensation at all. This creates a clear free-rider problem, in which a single large load subsidizes system transmission infrastructure that is subsequently used by a broad set of other customers who make no corresponding contribution.
As a result, the large load becomes the de facto financier of shared transmission infrastructure, while non-large loads receive the benefit of increased capacity and reliability without bearing any share of the cost. This outcome directly conflicts with the stated goal of ensuring that large loads pay only their fair share and instead results in system-wide subsidization by the very loads the rule is intended to regulate.
The Draft Rule also appears to contemplate allocating the cost of certain transmission facilities among multiple large loads on a “proportionate share” basis where those loads require the same line or upgrade. While this concept may appear intuitive, it is not technically workable or administratively defensible in the context of ERCOT’s contingency-based transmission planning process.
Transmission upgrades are justified across a wide range of contingency scenarios. A single upgrade may resolve thermal overloads in one contingency, voltage violations in another, and stability issues in a third, with different loads contributing to those violations in different cases. There is no stable or objective method to determine how much of a given line or upgrade is “used” by any particular load across these scenarios. Any attempt to assign proportional responsibility would necessarily rely on arbitrary assumptions, subjective weighting of contingencies, and continual recalculation as system conditions change.
This problem is amplified in a cluster-study planning environment, where transmission solutions are intentionally designed to serve groups of loads collectively rather than individual projects. Attempting to allocate proportional shares within a cluster undermines the premise of clustering and reintroduces the same project-by-project accounting complexity that cluster studies are intended to eliminate. By contrast, the existing ERCOT framework already addresses these issues effectively.
Historically:
Loads are required to post financial security (securitization) to cover the cost of transmission projects that are explicitly needed to serve them.
That security protects the TSP and ratepayers against stranded investment if the load fails to energize within a reasonable timeframe.
If the load does not materialize, the security is applied to actual, documented costs incurred.
This approach aligns with cost causation, avoids double recovery, prevents free-riding, and scales naturally as additional loads interconnect. It also integrates cleanly with both the current linear planning process and a future cluster-study paradigm, where upgrades are designed from the outset to serve multiple loads.

§25.194(h)(8): Financial Security as the Core of the Intermediate Agreement
Against this backdrop, §25.194(h)(8) should be the central and substantive provision of the Intermediate Agreement. Specifically, §25.194(h)(8) should make clear that the financial security posted under the Discretionary Services Agreement must first be applied to secure CIAC for direct-assigned facilities that serve only the requesting load; and securitization of network upgrades identified as necessary to serve the load.
If the security posted at the DSA stage is not used in this manner, it functions merely as a demonstration of the load’s ability to raise capital rather than as true security for facilities. A requirement to post “security” that does not actually secure construction costs is conceptually inconsistent with SB6’s authorization of financial commitment and may be difficult to defend if challenged.

§25.194(h)(9): Construction Progress, Permitting, and Load Advancement
For the same reasons, §25.194(h)(9)—which contemplates review of construction progress, permitting, or other non-electrical milestones—should either be revised to reflect existing ERCOT processes or struck entirely. Permitting status and construction sequencing are not reliable indicators of when electrical capacity will be required, and ERCOT and TSP staff do not have the expertise to interpret such information consistently. Introducing non-electrical milestones into the Intermediate Agreement risks confusion without improving transmission planning outcomes.
If the Commission determines that an update mechanism is necessary at this stage, it should be limited strictly to electrical ramping information. One workable alternative would be periodic updates identifying when the load expects to reach the next incremental level of electrical demand (for example, each additional 100 MW), continuing until full registered capacity is achieved.
It is also critical to recognize that registered capacity reflects expected demand during a 1-in-10-year extreme weather event. A site that reaches full build-out during a mild year may realize only 70–80% of registered capacity even though it is fully constructed and capable of reaching 100% under design conditions. Lower realized demand under non-extreme conditions should not be interpreted as lack of progress or non-compliance.
Cholla is concerned that the Draft Rule’s CIAC and Intermediate Agreement framework may be difficult to defend as a matter of cost causation, administrative feasibility, and future planning compatibility. These concerns are magnified as ERCOT transitions toward cluster studies, where shared transmission solutions and dynamic project information are essential. Preserving the historical distinction between direct-assigned facilities and shared network upgrades, relying on securitization rather than permanent CIAC for shared facilities, and confining the Intermediate Agreement to true financial and electrical commitments provides a durable, defensible, and future-proof framework consistent with SB6.

§25.194(i) Withdrawal, Reduction, and Treatment of Financial Security
PUC Subst. R. §25.194(i) should be structured to recognize two equally important realities:
Large load development plans can and do change for legitimate business reasons, and
there must be appropriate protections against stranded transmission investment where such changes leave unrecovered costs on the system.
These principles are not in conflict. When implemented correctly, they allow the interconnection process to remain flexible enough to support economic development while still protecting ratepayers and TSPs from unrecovered expenditures.
Support for §25.194(i)(1) and §25.194(i)(2)
Cholla generally supports §25.194(i)(1) and §25.194(i)(2), as these provisions appropriately recognize that changes to large-load interconnection requests can occur and that financial security should be applied in a manner tied to actual system impacts and incurred costs.
At the same time, Cholla recognizes that when a load materially reduces or withdraws its request, there may be transmission investments already underway that were predicated on that load’s participation. In those circumstances, it is appropriate for the withdrawing load to bear responsibility for actual, documented stranded costs that would not otherwise be recovered.
Accordingly, Cholla recommends that §25.194(i) provide that:
If a load reduces or withdraws a material portion of its requested capacity, the load shall forfeit the associated reserved transmission capacity; and
A study should be performed to determine whether any transmission investments have become stranded as a direct result of that reduction or withdrawal.
If such a study demonstrates that actual costs have been incurred and that those costs would not be recoverable absent the withdrawing load’s participation, then those costs may appropriately be deducted from the load’s posted financial security, consistent with long-standing practice.

Clarification to §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii): Equipment Cancellation or Reuse
Cholla recommends a narrow but important clarification to §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii) to ensure the provision remains consistent with cost-causation principles and reflects how transmission projects are executed in practice. Specifically, Cholla recommends that §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii) be revised to refer to facilities or equipment that are “canceled or reused.”
A substantial portion of the cost associated with transmission interconnection projects is tied to long-lead equipment, including transformers, breakers, structures, conductors, and other materials that are procured early in the project lifecycle. In many cases, if a project is canceled or reduced, that equipment is not stranded; instead, it is reused on other transmission projects, either to serve other interconnecting loads or to support broader system needs.
Where equipment or facilities are reused, the cost is not stranded, ratepayers are not harmed, and there is no cost-causation basis to charge the withdrawing load for that equipment.
Absent explicit recognition of reuse, §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii) could be interpreted to allow deduction of costs from a load’s security even where the underlying equipment continues to be productively deployed elsewhere on the system. That outcome would result in over-collection and would improperly penalize loads for investments that remain in service. Adding “or reused” makes clear that only costs associated with facilities or equipment that are canceled and not reused may be deducted from posted security. This clarification aligns the rule with existing ERCOT practice, protects against over-recovery, and ensures that financial security is applied only to actual, unrecovered stranded costs.
Consistent with the clarification above, security should not be forfeited when the transmission capacity made available by a withdrawal or reduction is immediately or near-immediately utilized by other loads. ERCOT is currently experiencing unprecedented load growth. In many cases, if one project steps back or exits the queue, multiple other projects are ready and willing to take its place. Where transmission capacity remains fully utilized, or where planned upgrades continue to be needed to serve other interconnecting loads, there is no stranded investment and no cost that should be allocated to the withdrawing project.

Strike §25.194(i)(3)
Cholla specifically recommends that §25.194(i)(3) be struck in its entirety. As drafted, subsection (i)(3) appears to impose forfeiture or penalty based on withdrawal or reduction alone, without requiring a showing of actual stranded costs or consideration of whether the transmission capacity continues to be used by other loads. Such an approach is unfair and difficult to defend, as it disconnects financial consequences from actual system impact. Penalizing a project simply for changing plans—without regard to whether any transmission investment has been stranded—violates fundamental cost-causation principles and creates outcomes that are arbitrary rather than corrective.
In an environment of rapid load growth, where transmission capacity is frequently reallocated almost immediately, subsection (i)(3) would result in systematic over-collection from withdrawing projects and effectively convert financial security into a punitive mechanism rather than a protective one. That result is inconsistent with the stated purpose of financial security under SB6. 
Cholla agrees that the Commission must preserve safeguards against stranded costs for a future environment in which load growth may slow or reverse. The protections embedded in §25.194(i) remain important in that context. However, those protections should be applied based on actual system impact, not automatically triggered by any reduction or withdrawal. The rule should be calibrated to today’s conditions while remaining flexible enough to function in a different future environment. This approach is also consistent with a cluster-study planning framework, where transmission solutions are designed to serve multiple loads collectively. In such an environment, the departure of a single project does not necessarily strand capacity; instead, that capacity is often absorbed by other cluster participants.
By tying forfeiture of security to demonstrated stranded costs, rather than to withdrawal alone, §25.194(i) can support orderly queue management without undermining the economic logic of clustering or imposing unnecessary penalties on projects that adjust their plans in good faith. Cholla recommends that §25.194(i) be implemented so that loads may reduce or withdraw their interconnection requests without penalty, except to the extent that their withdrawal results in actual stranded transmission costs that would not otherwise be recovered. Where capacity or equipment is reused by other loads or projects, no forfeiture of financial security should occur.
§25.194(j) Inactive or Stalled Projects
Cholla strongly supports §25.194(j). This provision addresses a long-standing and well-understood problem in transmission planning: the persistence of inactive or stalled interconnection requests that continue to occupy capacity and planning attention long after it has become clear that the underlying project is no longer advancing.
Removing these “zombie projects” from the system provides immediate and tangible benefits. It frees up transmission capacity for other loads that are prepared to move forward, reduces unnecessary restudies triggered by projects that are not viable, and allows ERCOT and the Transmission Service Providers to focus planning resources on projects that are actively progressing toward energization.
In the current environment of rapid load growth, this function is especially important. ERCOT is no longer operating in a system where load additions are scarce and every request must be preserved indefinitely. Instead, there is a deep pipeline of prospective loads, many of which are ready and able to use transmission capacity that may otherwise be blocked by inactive projects. §25.194(j) helps ensure that scarce transmission capacity is allocated to projects that can actually use it.
Cholla also supports §25.194(j) because it promotes more efficient use of the transmission system overall. Transmission planning is inherently forward-looking, and the presence of inactive projects in planning models distorts assumptions, delays decision-making, and can lead to over- or under-building of infrastructure. Clearing inactive projects from the queue improves model accuracy and results in better, more timely transmission solutions.
