Importantly, §25.194(j) complements—rather than conflicts with—the flexibility provided elsewhere in the rule. Projects that are actively advancing but need to adjust timing or scale are appropriately accommodated under §§25.194(f) and (i). By contrast, §25.194(j) is focused on projects that have ceased to progress and no longer justify continued reservation of capacity.

 §25.194(j) will materially improve the timely addition of load in ERCOT. By removing inactive projects and freeing capacity, this provision helps ensure that transmission infrastructure is put to productive use as quickly as possible, supporting economic development and system reliability alike.
For these reasons, Cholla strongly supports §25.194(j) as an essential tool for maintaining queue discipline, improving planning efficiency, and enabling the orderly integration of new load.
§25.194(k) Refund of Financial Security
Cholla supports the concept embodied in §25.194(k) that financial security should be refunded over time as load is energized and transmission facilities are placed into productive use. This approach appropriately recognizes that many large loads ramp gradually and that security should be released in a manner aligned with actual system utilization. That said, the refund framework as drafted is misaligned with real-world development timelines and would benefit from refinement. Large loads typically energize and ramp over extended periods. In many cases:
A project may not begin meaningful ramping for several years after interconnection approval,
Projects are often dependent on transmission upgrades that delay their full energization from their desired ramp schedule,
Full energization may not occur until ten years or more after initial studies, and
The ramp profile often reflects phased construction and commissioning cycles.
Against that backdrop, a refund structure that requires waiting five years after full energization before security is fully repaid is unnecessarily long and imposes a material financial burden that is disconnected from actual system risk. By the time a project has reached full energization, the transmission facilities serving it are already in use, the risk of non-performance has largely been eliminated, and the original purpose of the security—protecting against stranded investment—has been satisfied. Therefore a more appropriate and balanced approach would be to structure §25.194(k) so that full repayment of financial security occurs at or near full energization, rather than tying up capital after the security’s purpose has been fulfilled for several years afterward.
Need for Simplicity and Administrative Workability
While Cholla prefers a relatively simple refund mechanism, we also recognize that refund schedules must be administratively workable and reflect the diversity of project ramp profiles. Overly complex refund formulas increase administrative burden without improving outcomes. A refund structure tied to measurable electrical milestones—such as incremental MW energization and completion of full registered capacity—would provide clarity, predictability, and ease of administration while still protecting against stranded costs.
For these reasons, Cholla recommends that §25.194(k) be revised to allow for full repayment of financial security at full energization, with interim refunds aligned to ramping milestones, rather than requiring an additional multi-year waiting period after full load is achieved.

§25.194(l) Reliability Standards Applicable to Large Loads
Cholla understands the desire reflected in §25.194(l) to provide ERCOT with tools to ensure that large loads operate in a manner consistent with system reliability, including compliance with standards such as low voltage ride through (LVRT) and other dynamic performance requirements. Cholla recognizes that as large loads become a more material portion of total ERCOT demand, their behavior during system disturbances is increasingly important to overall grid stability. Cholla does not take a position in these comments on the legal authority of the Commission or ERCOT to directly impose or enforce such standards on loads. Instead, Cholla focuses on the practical and technical realities of how reliability issues such as LVRT are most effectively addressed.
It is critical to recognize that solutions to issues such as LVRT do not lie solely with the load. In such a framework, it becomes easy to assign increasingly stringent or burdensome obligations to one group, even where the most effective solution would involve a combination of load-side changes, transmission upgrades, or other system-level investments. In practice, achieving desired system performance during voltage disturbances is a combination of measures, which may include:
Modifications to load-side controls, such as the configuration and control logic of uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) in data centers;
Coordination and control of backup generation systems, including how and when those systems respond to voltage events;
Installation of devices or upgrades on the transmission system itself, such as reactive support, protection adjustments, or other grid-side solutions; and
Coordinated operational strategies that consider the interaction of loads, generation, and transmission facilities during fault conditions.
Focusing exclusively on load-side compliance risks overlooking solutions that may be more efficient, more reliable, or lower cost when implemented elsewhere on the system. Loads should be incentivized to make reasonable corrections and upgrades where those actions are cost-effective and directly address the reliability concern at issue. At the same time, where system-level solutions are more efficient, those options should be considered holistically. 
One possible approach is the development of services or solutions designed specifically to address reliability needs such as voltage ride-through performance, with costs allocated to large loads based on cost-causation principles. Under such a framework, large loads would contribute to reliability improvements in proportion to the benefit received or the impact caused, rather than being required to implement all solutions unilaterally.
As a guiding principle, if ERCOT were an integrated utility tasked with solving this problem internally, it would evaluate the full range of available options—load-side changes, transmission investments, operational strategies—and select the combination that achieves reliability at the lowest total system cost. The regulatory and market framework should strive to allow the ERCOT market to produce those same efficient outcomes, rather than defaulting to a model that places the full burden of reliability compliance on a single category of customers. Reliability standards should therefore be implemented in a manner that is coordinated, proportionate, and aligned with system-wide efficiency.

CIAC, Network Upgrades, and “Fair Share” Cost Allocation

       Cholla understands and supports the underlying policy objective reflected in SB6: ensuring

that large loads pay their fair share of transmission costs associated with serving them. However,

CIAC is not the appropriate mechanism to achieve that objective, and Cholla does not find

anything in SB6 requiring or supporting the use of CIAC to replace or replicate system-wide

transmission cost recovery. SB6 explicitly directed the Commission to review transmission cost

allocation rules, including the Four Coincident Peak (4CP) mechanism, as the appropriate vehicle

for addressing concerns about whether large loads are contributing proportionately to the

transmission system. That directive reflects a recognition that system transmission costs are best

allocated through system-wide rate design, not through project-specific CIAC constructs.




                                                                                                  38
 Attempting to force “fair share” cost recovery through CIAC creates a series of fundamental

problems.

       First, CIAC is incompatible with ongoing TCOS recovery. If a large load is required to

fund the bulk of a transmission upgrade through CIAC, it is not economically or legally coherent

to then also charge that same load ongoing TCOS based on 4CP or other system metrics. Doing so

would result in reverse subsidization, where the load both pays for the asset upfront and continues

to pay for it again through rates, while other users benefit without equivalent contribution.

       Second, the Draft Rule’s attempt to address this issue through a concept of subsequent

compensation by later-connecting large loads is not workable. Transmission facilities are

constructed to satisfy multiple contingency cases across a wide range of system conditions.

Determining “how much” of a line or upgrade is used by a second or third load across dozens or

hundreds of contingencies would require arbitrary allocation assumptions, highly subjective

modeling judgments, and continual recalculation as new loads interconnect. This quickly devolves

into an incomprehensible accounting exercise, with no clear answer as to how compensation would

be calculated, tracked, or revisited over time.

       Third, and equally problematic, the Draft Rule’s compensation construct appears to apply

only to subsequent large loads. Under this approach, only later-connecting large loads would be

required to compensate the original load that funded the upgrade, while all other loads—including

smaller commercial, industrial, and residential customers—would use the upgraded transmission

facilities without providing any compensation at all. This creates a clear free-rider problem, in

which a single large load subsidizes system transmission infrastructure that is subsequently used

by a broad set of other customers who make no corresponding contribution.




                                                                                                39
         As a result, the large load becomes the de facto financier of shared transmission

infrastructure, while non-large loads receive the benefit of increased capacity and reliability

without bearing any share of the cost. This outcome directly conflicts with the stated goal of

ensuring that large loads pay only their fair share and instead results in system-wide subsidization

by the very loads the rule is intended to regulate.

        The Draft Rule also appears to contemplate allocating the cost of certain transmission

facilities among multiple large loads on a “proportionate share” basis where those loads require

the same line or upgrade. While this concept may appear intuitive, it is not technically workable

or administratively defensible in the context of ERCOT’s contingency-based transmission

planning process.

        Transmission upgrades are justified across a wide range of contingency scenarios. A single

upgrade may resolve thermal overloads in one contingency, voltage violations in another, and

stability issues in a third, with different loads contributing to those violations in different cases.

There is no stable or objective method to determine how much of a given line or upgrade is “used”

by any particular load across these scenarios. Any attempt to assign proportional responsibility

would necessarily rely on arbitrary assumptions, subjective weighting of contingencies, and

continual recalculation as system conditions change.

        This problem is amplified in a cluster-study planning environment, where transmission

solutions are intentionally designed to serve groups of loads collectively rather than individual

projects. Attempting to allocate proportional shares within a cluster undermines the premise of

clustering and reintroduces the same project-by-project accounting complexity that cluster studies

are intended to eliminate. By contrast, the existing ERCOT framework already addresses these

issues effectively.

In such a framework, it becomes easy to assign increasingly stringent or burdensome obligations

to one group, even where the most effective solution would involve a combination of load-side

   •   Modifications to load-side controls, such as the configuration and control logic of

       uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) in data centers;

   •   Coordination and control of backup generation systems, including how and when those

   •   Installation of devices or upgrades on the transmission system itself, such as reactive

    •   Coordinated operational strategies that consider the interaction of loads, generation, and

reliability at the lowest total system cost. The regulatory and market framework should strive to

allow the ERCOT market to produce those same efficient outcomes, rather than defaulting to a

model that places the full burden of reliability compliance on a single category of customers.

Reliability standards should therefore be implemented in a manner that is coordinated,

proportionate, and aligned with system-wide efficiency.

CIAC. Network Upgrades. and "Fair Share" Cost Allocation


       Cholla understands and supports the underlying policy objective reflected in SB6: ensuring

that large loads pay their fair share of transmission costs associated with serving them. However,

CIAC is not the appropriate mechanism to achieve that objective, and Cholla does not find

anything in SB6 requiring or supporting the use of CIAC to replace or replicate system-wide

transmission cost recovery. SB6 explicitly directed the Commission to review transmission cost

allocation rules, including the Four Coincident Peak (4CP) mechanism, as the appropriate vehicle

for addressing concerns about whether large loads are contributing proportionately to the

transmission system. That directive reflects a recognition that system transmission costs are best

allocated through system-wide rate design, not through project-specific CIAC constructs.

Attempting to force "fair share" cost recovery through CIAC creates a series of fundamental

problems.




                                                                                                  38
        First, CIAC is incompatible with ongoing TCOS recovery. If a large load is required to

fund the bulk of a transmission upgrade through CIAC, it is not economically or legally coherent

to then also charge that same load ongoing TCOS based on 4CP or other system metrics. Doing so

would result in reverse subsidization, where the load both pays for the asset upfront and continues

to pay for it again through rates, while other users benefit without equivalent contribution.


        Second, the Draft Rule' s attempt to address this issue through a concept of subsequent

compensation by later-connecting large loads is not workable. Transmission facilities are

constructed to satisfy multiple contingency cases across a wide range of system conditions.

Determining "how much" of a line or upgrade is used by a second or third load across dozens or

hundreds of contingencies would require arbitrary allocation assumptions, highly subjective

modeling judgments, and continual recalculation as new loads interconnect. This quickly devolves

into an incomprehensible accounting exercise, with no clear answer as to how compensation would

be calculated, tracked, or revisited over time.


       Third, and equally problematic, the Draft Rule' s compensation construct appears to apply

only to subsequent large loads. Under this approach, only later-connecting large loads would be

required to compensate the original load that funded the upgrade, while all other loads-including

smaller commercial, industrial, and residential customers-would use the upgraded transmission

facilities without providing any compensation at all. This creates a clear free-rider problem, in

which a single large load subsidizes system transmission infrastructure that is subsequently used

by a broad set of other customers who make no corresponding contribution.


       As a result, the large load becomes the de facto financier of shared transmission

infrastructure, while non-large loads receive the benefit of increased capacity and reliability

without bearing any share of the cost. This outcome directly conflicts with the stated goal of


                                                                                                39
 ensuring that large loads pay only their fair share and instead results in system-wide subsidization

by the very loads the rule is intended to regulate.


        The Draft Rule also appears to contemplate allocating the cost of certain transmission

facilities among multiple large loads on a "proportionate share" basis where those loads require

the same line or upgrade. While this concept may appear intuitive, it is not technically workable

or administratively defensible in the context of ERCOT's contingency-based transmission

planning process.


        Transmission upgrades are justified across a wide range of contingency scenarios. A single

upgrade may resolve thermal overloads in one contingency, voltage violations in another, and

stability issues in a third, with different loads contributing to those violations in different cases.

There is no stable or objective method to determine how much of a given line or upgrade is "used"

by any particular load across these scenarios. Any attempt to assign proportional responsibility

would necessarily rely on arbitrary assumptions, subjective weighting of contingencies, and

continual recalculation as system conditions change.


        This problem is amplified in a cluster-study planning environment, where transmission

solutions are intentionally designed to serve groups of loads collectively rather than individual

projects. Attempting to allocate proportional shares within a cluster undermines the premise of

clustering and reintroduces the same project-by-project accounting complexity that cluster studies

are intended to eliminate. By contrast, the existing ERCOT framework already addresses these

issues effectively.


Historically:

CIAC, Network Upgrades, and "Fair Share" Cost Allocation


       Cholla understands and supports the underlying policy objective reflected in SB6: ensuring

that large loads pay their fair share of transmission costs associated with serving them. However,

CIAC is not the appropriate mechanism to achieve that objective, and Cholla does not find

anything in SB6 requiring or supporting the use of CIAC to replace or replicate system-wide

transmission cost recovery. SB6 explicitly directed the Commission to review transmission cost

allocation rules, including the Four Coincident Peak (4CP) mechanism, as the appropriate vehicle

for addressing concerns about whether large loads are contributing proportionately to the

transmission system. That directive reflects a recognition that system transmission costs are best

allocated through system-wide rate design, not through project-specific CIAC constructs.




                                                                                                  38
 Attempting to force "fair share" cost recovery through CIAC creates a series of fundamental

problems.

       First, CIAC is incompatible with ongoing TCOS recovery. If a large load is required to

fund the bulk of a transmission upgrade through CIAC, it is not economically or legally coherent

to then also charge that same load ongoing TCOS based on 4CP or other system metrics. Doing so

would result in reverse subsidization, where the load both pays for the asset upfront and continues

to pay for it again through rates, while other users benefit without equivalent contribution.


        Second, the Draft Rule's attempt to address this issue through a concept of subsequent

compensation by later-connecting large loads is not workable. Transmission facilities are

constructed to satisfy multiple contingency cases across a wide range of system conditions.

Determining "how much" of a line or upgrade is used by a second or third load across dozens or

hundreds of contingencies would require arbitrary allocation assumptions, highly subjective

modeling judgments, and continual recalculation as new loads interconnect. This quickly devolves

into an incomprehensible accounting exercise, with no clear answer as to how compensation would

be calculated, tracked, or revisited over time.


       Third, and equally problematic, the Draft Rule's compensation construct appears to apply

only to subsequent large loads. Under this approach, only later-connecting large loads would be

required to compensate the original load that funded the upgrade, while all other loads-including

smaller commercial, industrial, and residential customers-would use the upgraded transmission

facilities without providing any compensation at all. This creates a clear free-rider problem, in

which a single large load subsidizes system transmission infrastructure that is subsequently used

by a broad set of other customers who make no corresponding contribution.




                                                                                                39
         As a result, the large load becomes the de facto financier of shared transmission

infrastructure, while non-large loads receive the benefit of increased capacity and reliability

without bearing any share of the cost. This outcome directly conflicts with the stated goal of

ensuring that large loads pay only their fair share and instead results in system-wide subsidization

by the very loads the rule is intended to regulate.


        The Draft Rule also appears to contemplate allocating the cost of certain transmission

facilities among multiple large loads on a "proportionate share" basis where those loads require

the same line or upgrade. While this concept may appear intuitive, it is not technically workable

or administratively defensible in the context of ERCOT's contingency-based transmission

planning process.


        Transmission upgrades are justified across a wide range of contingency scenarios. A single

upgrade may resolve thermal overloads in one contingency, voltage violations in another, and

stability issues in a third, with different loads contributing to those violations in different cases.

There is no stable or objective method to determine how much of a given line or upgrade is "used"

by any particular load across these scenarios. Any attempt to assign proportional responsibility

would necessarily rely on arbitrary assumptions, subj ective weighting of contingencies, and

continual recalculation as system conditions change.


        This problem is amplified in a cluster-study planning environment, where transmission

solutions are intentionally designed to serve groups of loads collectively rather than individual

projects. Attempting to allocate proportional shares within a cluster undermines the premise of

clustering and reintroduces the same proj ect-by-proj ect accounting complexity that cluster studies

are intended to eliminate. By contrast, the existing ERCOT framework already addresses these

issues effectively.


                                                                                                   40
 Historically:


    •   Loads are required to post financial security (securitization) to cover the cost of

        transmission proj ects that are explicitly needed to serve them.

    •   That security protects the TSP and ratepayers against stranded investment if the load fails

        to energize within a reasonable timeframe.

    •   Ifthe load does not materialize, the security is applied to actual, documented costs incurred.


    This approach aligns with cost causation, avoids double recovery, prevents free-riding, and

scales naturally as additional loads interconnect. It also integrates cleanly with both the current

linear planning process and a future cluster-study paradigm, where upgrades are designed from the

outset to serve multiple loads.

the Intermediate Agreement to true financial and electrical commitments provides a durable,

defensible, and future-proof framework consistent with SB6.




§25.194(i) Withdrawal, Reduction, and Treatment of Financial Security


PUC Subst. R. §25. 194(i) should be structured to recognize two equally important realities:


       (1) Large load development plans can and do change for legitimate business reasons, and

       (2) there must be appropriate protections against stranded transmission investment where

           such changes leave unrecovered costs on the system.


       These principles are not in conflict. When implemented correctly, they allow the

interconnection process to remain flexible enough to support economic development while still

protecting ratepayers and TSPs from unrecovered expenditures.


Support for §25.194(i)(1) and §25.194(i)(2)


       Cholla generally supports §25.194(i)(1) and §25.194(i)(2), as these provisions

appropriately recognize that changes to large-load interconnection requests can occur and that

financial security should be applied in a manner tied to actual system impacts and incurred costs.


       At the same time, Cholla recognizes that when a load materially reduces or withdraws its

request, there may be transmission investments already underway that were predicated on that

load's participation. In those circumstances, it is appropriate for the withdrawing load to bear

responsibility for actual, documented stranded costs that would not otherwise be recovered.



                                                                                                43
    Accordingly, Cholla recommends that §25. 194(i) provide that:


   •   If a load reduces or withdraws a material portion of its requested capacity, the load shall

       forfeit the associated reserved transmission capacity; and

   •   A study should be performed to determine whether any transmission investments have

       become stranded as a direct result of that reduction or withdrawal.


   If such a study demonstrates that actual costs have been incurred and that those costs would

not be recoverable absent the withdrawing load's participation, then those costs may appropriately

be deducted from the load's posted financial security, consistent with long-standing practice.




Clarification to §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii): Equipment Cancellation or Reuse


       Cholla recommends a narrow but important clarification to §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii) to ensure

the provision remains consistent with cost-causation principles and reflects how transmission

projects are executed in practice. Specifically, Cholla recommends that §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii) be

revised to refer to facilities or equipment that are "canceled or reused."


       A substantial portion of the cost associated with transmission interconnection proj ects is

tied to long-lead equipment, including transformers, breakers, structures, conductors, and other

materials that are procured early in the project lifecycle. In many cases, if a project is canceled or

reduced, that equipment is not stranded; instead, it is reused on other transmission proj ects, either

to serve other interconnecting loads or to support broader system needs.


   Where equipment or facilities are reused, the cost is not stranded, ratepayers are not harmed,

and there is no cost-causation basis to charge the withdrawing load for that equipment.




                                                                                                   44
    Absent explicit recognition of reuse, §25.194(i)(2)(A)(ii) could be interpreted to allow

deduction of costs from a load's security even where the underlying equipment continues to be

productively deployed elsewhere on the system. That outcome would result in over-collection and

would improperly penalize loads for investments that remain in service . Adding "or reused "

makes clear that only costs associated with facilities or equipment that are canceled and not reused

may be deducted from posted security. This clarification aligns the rule with existing ERCOT

practice, protects against over-recovery, and ensures that financial security is applied only to

actual, unrecovered stranded costs.


       Consistent with the clarification above, security should not be forfeited when the

transmission capacity made available by a withdrawal or reduction is immediately or near-

immediately utilized by other loads. ERCOT is currently experiencing unprecedented load growth.

In many cases, if one proj ect steps back or exits the queue, multiple other proj ects are ready and

willing to take its place. Where transmission capacity remains fully utilized, or where planned

upgrades continue to be needed to serve other interconnecting loads, there is no stranded

investment and no cost that should be allocated to the withdrawing proj ect.




Strike §25.194(i)(3)


       Cholla specifically recommends that §25.194(i)(3) be struck in its entirety. As drafted,

subsection (i)(3) appears to impose forfeiture or penalty based on withdrawal or reduction alone,

without requiring a showing of actual stranded costs or consideration of whether the transmission

capacity continues to be used by other loads. Such an approach is unfair and difficult to defend, as

it disconnects financial consequences from actual system impact. Penalizing a project simply for




                                                                                                 45
 changing plans-without regard to whether any transmission investment has been stranded-

violates fundamental cost-causation principles and creates outcomes that are arbitrary rather than

corrective.


       In an environment of rapid load growth, where transmission capacity is frequently

reallocated almost immediately, subsection (i)(3) would result in systematic over-collection from

withdrawing projects and effectively convert financial security into a punitive mechanism rather

than a protective one. That result is inconsistent with the stated purpose of financial security under

SB6.

        Cholla agrees that the Commission must preserve safeguards against stranded costs for a

future environment in which load growth may slow or reverse. The protections embedded in

§25.194(i) remain important in that context. However, those protections should be applied based

on actual system impact, not automatically triggered by any reduction or withdrawal. The rule

should be calibrated to today's conditions while remaining flexible enough to function in a

different future environment. This approach is also consistent with a cluster-study planning

framework, where transmission solutions are designed to serve multiple loads collectively. In such

an environment, the departure of a single proj ect does not necessarily strand capacity; instead, that

capacity is often absorbed by other cluster participants.


       By tying forfeiture of security to demonstrated stranded costs, rather than to withdrawal

alone, §25.194(i) can support orderly queue management without undermining the economic logic

of clustering or imposing unnecessary penalties on projects that adjust their plans in good faith.

Cholla recommends that §25.194(i) be implemented so that loads may reduce or withdraw their

interconnection requests without penalty, except to the extent that their withdrawal results in actual

stranded transmission costs that would not otherwise be recovered. Where capacity or equipment

is reused by other loads or projects, no forfeiture of financial security should occur.


§25.194(i) Inactive or Stalled Proiects


          Cholla strongly supports §25.194(j). This provision addresses a long-standing and well-

understood problem in transmission planning: the persistence of inactive or stalled interconnection

requests that continue to occupy capacity and planning attention long after it has become clear that

the underlying project is no longer advancing.


          Removing these "zombie projects" from the system provides immediate and tangible

benefits. It frees up transmission capacity for other loads that are prepared to move forward,

reduces unnecessary restudies triggered by proj ects that are not viable, and allows ERCOT and the

Transmission Service Providers to focus planning resources on projects that are actively

progressing toward energization.


          In the current environment of rapid load growth, this function is especially important.

ERCOT is no longer operating in a system where load additions are scarce and every request must

be preserved indefinitely. Instead, there is a deep pipeline of prospective loads, many ofwhich are

ready and able to use transmission capacity that may otherwise be blocked by inactive projects.

§25.194(j) helps ensure that scarce transmission capacity is allocated to projects that can actually

use it.


          Cholla also supports §25.194(j) because it promotes more efficient use of the transmission

system overall. Transmission planning is inherently forward-looking, and the presence of inactive

projects in planning models distorts assumptions, delays decision-making, and can lead to over-

§25.194(k) Refund of Financial Security


         Cholla supports the concept embodied in §25.194(k) that financial security should be

refunded over time as load is energized and transmission facilities are placed into productive use.

This approach appropriately recognizes that many large loads ramp gradually and that security

should be released in a manner aligned with actual system utilization. That said, the refund

framework as drafted is misaligned with real-world development timelines and would benefit from

refinement. Large loads typically energize and ramp over extended periods. In many cases:


•    A proj ect may not begin meaningful ramping for several years after interconnection approval,




                                                                                                   48
 •   Projects are often dependent on transmission upgrades that delay their full energization from

    their desired ramp schedule,

•   Full energization may not occur until ten years or more after initial studies, and

•   The ramp profile often reflects phased construction and commissioning cycles.


    Against that backdrop, a refund structure that requires waiting five years after full energization

before security is fully repaid is unnecessarily long and imposes a material financial burden that is

disconnected from actual system risk. By the time a project has reached full energization, the

transmission facilities serving it are already in use, the risk of non-performance has largely been

eliminated, and the original purpose of the security-protecting against stranded investment-has

been satisfied. Therefore a more appropriate and balanced approach would be to structure

§25.194(k) so that full repayment of financial security occurs at or near full energization, rather

than tying up capital after the security's purpose has been fulfilled for several years afterward.


Need for Simplicity and Administrative Workabilitv


       While Cholla prefers a relatively simple refund mechanism, we also recognize that refund

schedules must be administratively workable and reflect the diversity of project ramp profiles.

Overly complex refund formulas increase administrative burden without improving outcomes. A

refund structure tied to measurable electrical milestones-such as incremental MW energization

and completion of full registered capacity-would provide clarity, predictability, and ease of

administration while still protecting against stranded costs.


For these reasons, Cholla recommends that §25.194(k) be revised to allow for full repayment of

financial security at full energization, with interim refunds aligned to ramping milestones, rather

than requiring an additional multi-year waiting period after fullload is achieved.

 §25.194(1) Reliability Standards Applicable to Large Loads


       Cholla understands the desire reflected in §25.194(1) to provide ERCOT with tools to

ensure that large loads operate in a manner consistent with system reliability, including compliance

with standards such as low voltage ride through *VRT) and other dynamic performance

requirements. Cholla recognizes that as large loads become a more material portion of total

ERCOT demand, their behavior during system disturbances is increasingly important to overall

grid stability. Cholla does not take a position in these comments on the legal authority of the

Commission or ERCOT to directly impose or enforce such standards on loads. Instead, Cholla

focuses on the practical and technical realities of how reliability issues such as LVRT are most

effectively addressed.


   It is critical to recognize that solutions to issues such as LVRT do not lie solely with the load.

In such a framework, it becomes easy to assign increasingly stringent or burdensome obligations

to one group, even where the most effective solution would involve a combination of load-side

changes, transmission upgrades, or other system-level investments. In practice, achieving desired

system performance during voltage disturbances is a combination ofmeasures, which may include:


   •   Modifications to load-side controls, such as the configuration and control logic of

       uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) in data centers;

   •   Coordination and control of backup generation systems, including how and when those

       systems respond to voltage events;

   •   Installation of devices or upgrades on the transmission system itself, such as reactive

       support, protection adjustments, or other grid-side solutions; and



                                                                                                  50
    •   Coordinated operational strategies that consider the interaction of loads, generation, and

       transmission facilities during fault conditions.


   Focusing exclusively on load-side compliance risks overlooking solutions that may be more

efficient, more reliable, or lower cost when implemented elsewhere on the system. Loads should

be incentivized to make reasonable corrections and upgrades where those actions are cost-effective

and directly address the reliability concern at issue. At the same time, where system-level solutions

are more efficient, those options should be considered holistically.


       One possible approach is the development of services or solutions designed specifically to

address reliability needs such as voltage ride-through performance, with costs allocated to large

loads based on cost-causation principles. Under such a framework, large loads would contribute

to reliability improvements in proportion to the benefit received or the impact caused, rather than

being required to implement all solutions unilaterally.


       As a guiding principle, if ERCOT were an integrated utility tasked with solving this

problem internally, it would evaluate the full range of available options-load-side changes,

transmission investments, operational strategies-and select the combination that achieves

reliability at the lowest total system cost. The regulatory and market framework should strive to

allow the ERCOT market to produce those same efficient outcomes, rather than defaulting to a

model that places the full burden of reliability compliance on a single category of customers.

Reliability standards should therefore be implemented in a manner that is coordinated,

proportionate, and aligned with system-wide efficiency.
